detail.abstract: Restrepo (2025) shows that once artificial general intelligence lets compute perform every task, output becomes linear in compute, wages converge to the value of the compute a worker saves, and the labor share goes to zero. We extend his task economy by treating compute as a reproducible, priced, depreciating capital good that needs energy and works alongside structures and land, and by adding households that own the claims to income. The labor-share result survives any constant-returns production structure: it needs only within-task substitutability. The wage-level result does not: when physical complements are gross complements and compute becomes cheap, the price of compute and wages go to zero in level and the income that labor loses goes to the owners of the scarcest complement; with a floor on the compute price, the wage equals the user cost of the replacement compute. Income shares and asset values are different objects: compute is capitalized at the duration of chips, so capital's share can rise while the wealth-to-income ratio falls, and a growth boom raises the real rate and compresses valuation ratios when the elasticity of intertemporal substitution is below one. In a calibrated model solved along perfect-foresight paths to 2300 under conditional scenarios, the labor share falls to 0.283 by 2050, the real return peaks at 40.5%, the wealth-to-income ratio falls to 2.7 before land captures 0.605 of income and raises it to 31.0 by 2100, and the market value of compute never exceeds one fifth of GDP. A compute tax raises wages one-for-one with the tax-inclusive user cost; a land tax redistributes without distortion; a citizen fund keeps workers' consumption share bounded away from zero.

detail.abstract:
When machines can fake, make and imitate almost anything, what is left that only a human being can do?

The Other Ledger followed the rest of the money. The Last Arena follows the parts of life people have long believed only people could supply: the truth they tell each other, the stories they watch, the art they make, and the contests they play. It is built as a funnel. Machines take much of the news by faking it, much of the film studio by making it and much of the art market by imitating it. What is left, at the narrow end, is the arena, where the human body is the whole of what people watch, even as the ball, the referee and the broadcast are made or run by machines.

Drawing on court cases and new laws from Hollywood to Mumbai, the economics of journalism, film, music and sport, and five models tested against public data, it shows that what survives the machines survives only if its audience can afford it, and that the audience's income depends on who owns the machines. Each chapter states the strongest objection to its own argument and what would show it wrong.

Told through Ruth Calloway, the editor of the town's paper, Marcus Bell, a camera operator who spent twelve years on film crews, and Jordan, who coached the under-twelves until the pitch closed, alongside Daniel from the first three books, it follows one town from the evening the news put the machines ninth, after the weather, to the night of a World Cup final watched by three hundred people in a carpet warehouse.

The last arena stays human only on a road where people can still afford to watch it.

detail.abstract:
When machines take most of the work, the money does not disappear — it moves. The Other Ledger follows where it goes.

This book examines the economic and institutional consequences of advanced artificial intelligence and robotics beyond the labour market itself. It tracks the reallocation of income, capital, and fiscal capacity once large parts of production no longer require human wages. The analysis centres on three questions that run through the entire series: Who earns? Who pays? What does the state gain or lose?

The book develops and applies several core frames, including the Wage Shadow, the Circularity Trap, and the distinction between the Owners’ Road, the State’s Road, and the Shared Road. It shows how ownership of the machines determines whether the gains concentrate, are captured by the state, or are distributed more widely, and how each path reshapes tax bases, demand, and institutional stability.

The Other Ledger is a work of hybrid nonfiction. It combines institutional and economic analysis with carefully marked narrative scenes, states the strongest objections to its own arguments, and tests key claims against available data. It forms the first volume of Part 2 of The Next Human Epoch, running parallel to the earlier trilogy on work, money, and the nation.

The book is written for readers who want a clear, evidence-based account of how the money moves when human labour is no longer the central organising principle of production — and what that movement implies for ownership, the state, and the residual human economy.

detail.abstract: This working paper attempts to examine how machine learning, natural language processing and generative models are being embedded into marketing decisions. The examination moves the discipline from periodic, campaign-led planning toward continuous, evidence-based optimization. The study reviews the technological foundations of AI-enabled marketing, describes the data architecture that supports it. The working also proposes to analyses six major application areas for evaluation. These domains are recommendation and personalization, predictive scoring, programmatic advertising and attribution, conversational interfaces, generative content production, and dynamic pricing. Illustrative implementations from streaming, retail, beverages, beauty and business-to-business (B2B) software are discussed to show how these tools operate in practice. The paper also evaluates the risks that accompany adoption, including privacy exposure, embedded bias, model opacity, uneven access to capital and talent, and the temptation to manipulate rather than serve consumers. It concludes that durable advantage will not come from the sophistication of algorithms alone. It will come from organizations that pair automated decision systems with human judgment, treat customer data as a trust obligation, and measure success by long-term customer value rather than short-term click behaviour.

detail.abstract: Following the withdrawal of Western multinational corporations from Russia after 2022, this paper analyzes how persistent brand equity affects the viability of domestic substitutes. It distinguishes functional substitutability, based on practical utility, from symbolic substitutability, based on prestige, trust, and authenticity. Using behavioral economics literature and indexed, inflation-adjusted revenue data from 2019-2024, it compares McDonald's/Vkusno i Tochka with Coca-Cola/Dobriy Cola. Vkusno i Tochka recovered towards pre-pandemic revenue levels, whereas Dobriy Cola remained substantially below its baseline. This divergence suggests that familiar functions and consumption routines can support domestic successors, while symbolic loyalty and continued access to original products can constrain substitution. The paper conceptualizes the persistent influence of Western brands as "ghost infrastructure", sustained by alternative distribution routes and consumer perceptions. Although the descriptive comparison cannot establish causality, the findings suggest that successful import substitution depends on brand value transferability and accessibility of alternative distribution networks.

detail.abstract:
Background & Purpose: Consumer dining habits are changing in emerging markets, and this calls for a holistic view of the dining service experience. The study asks how Integrated Service Quality (ISQ), a Formative High-Order Construct (HOC), shapes consumer Repurchase Intention (RI) in the fast-food restaurant industry (FFRI) in Vietnam. It also tests the dual mediating roles of Perceived Value (PV) and Brand Image (BI) within an extended Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-OR) framework that draws on Signaling Theory and Customer Based Brand Equity (CBBE). 

Methodology: A sequential mixed-methods design was used. Preliminary qualitative work with 16 domain experts and 27 consumers refined the measurement scales first. The main quantitative phase then collected data from 415 fast-food consumers in three major economic regions of Vietnam (Ho Chi Minh City, Can Tho and Hue). Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) served to examine the two-stage reflective-formative measurement model and the structural path relationships, and bootstrapping with 5,000 resamples tested the mediation effects. 

Findings: All six lower-order reflective dimensions showed statistically significant formative weights (p < 0.001) in forming the second-order ISQ construct: Responsiveness (w = 0.201), Food Quality (w = 0.228), Individualized Attention (w = 0.187), Service Competence (w = 0.214), Interior Design (w = 0.198), and Perceived Omnichannel Seamlessness (w = 0.209). The structural analysis showed that ISQ had a significant direct effect on Repurchase Intention (β = 0.381, p < 0.001). The mediation analysis showed that Perceived Value and Brand Image partially mediate the relationship between ISQ and RI. Two parallel paths were significant, one through Brand Image (β = 0.122, p < 0.001) and one through Perceived Value (β = 0.147, p < 0.001), together with a serial path from ISQ through Perceived Value and Brand Image to RI (β = 0.074, p < 0.001). 

Theoretical & Managerial Implications: The study adds to the SO -R paradigm by operationalizing service quality as a second-order formative construct that brings physical and digital touchpoints together in an emerging-market setting. On the managerial side, it guides FFR executives on how spatial interior design, frontline staff competencies, and omnichannel integration can be used to retain shoppers in the city.

detail.abstract: Generation Z consumers are frequent targets of AI-personalized Buy-One-Get-One (BOGO) promotions, yet little is known about how trust and awareness of AI personalization relate to their responses in underserved Philippine settings. This study examined how Digital Trust (website/platform trust, security and privacy) and AI Personalization Awareness (perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use) relate to Generation Z consumers' responses (purchase intention, engagement with promotion) to AI-personalized BOGO promotions at Bukidnon State University-Talisayan Campus, Misamis Oriental. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was used: a fourpoint Likert-scale questionnaire (Cronbach's alpha = 0.985) was administered to 192 students, followed by interviews with ten purposively selected key informants. Respondents reported High Digital Trust (M = 2.97), Awareness of AI personalization (M = 2.91), and High consumer response (M = 2.96), with engagement with promotion (M = 3.07) exceeding purchase intention (M = 2.85). Digital Trust (r = .806, p < .001) and AI Personalization Awareness (r = .817, p < .001) were each strongly and significantly related to consumer response. Thematic analysis identified four suggestions: physical product quality, more frequent promotions, prevention of visual scams, and consistent social media posting. The results are correlational and drawn from a single campus. They suggest that trust attaches to the seller and the product as well as the platform, and that AI-personalized offers should be paired with visible security cues, accurate product presentation, and clear explanations of why a deal is recommended.

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become one of the most promising technologies in contemporary marketing management. Artificial intelligence can help organizations to analyze vast amounts of customer data, identify patterns, recognize customer preferences and offer relevant products, services and information. In particular, AI-driven customer personalization has become one of the most in-demand concepts, as customers seek greater relevance in terms of products, content, offers and communication. This project aims to review the concept of Customer Personalization in Marketing driven by Artificial Intelligence, discussing such aspects as AI-based customer segmentation and targeting, personalized recommendation and predictive marketing, AI-generated content and advertising, AI chatbots and conversational marketing, benefits, challenges and future of AI-driven personalization. Particular attention is paid to the role of AI in the customer journey, its impact on marketing management, the application of AI in different spheres, and ethical concerns related to privacy, security, bias and hyper-personalization. The study finds that AI can be a powerful tool for marketing management, helping to make operations more efficient, engage and retain customers, identify and target the right customers, and make better business decisions. However, the effectiveness of AI is conditional upon high-quality data, responsibility, privacy and transparency, and human oversight. Thus, while AI can be a great tool for marketing management, it cannot replace human input in marketing management. The project also concludes that the future of marketing belongs to marketing management that combines artificial intelligence, customer data and human expertise to meet the needs of customers and ensure long-term success.

detail.abstract: For an AI data center awaiting grid expansion, early electricity access offers the opportunity to begin operating sooner, but only if the computation deferred to secure that access can subsequently be recovered within shared capacity. We study this admission problem for a fixed cohort with certified, energy-conserving operating modes, public connection values, and independent regular private flexibility costs, using scalar screening to implement the ratepayer-optimal allocation. Comparing counterfactual capacity states, we bound an unchanged workload profile's opportunity-price increase and admission-cutoff contraction by the loss from requiring a common competing recovery portfolio; sharp examples reveal that capacity expansion can nearly eliminate an applicant's access probability even as aggregate expected benefit rises. For menu simplification, re-optimized dual prices identify certificate conservatism exactly as an LP integrality gap, which disappears under disjoint proportional recovery blocks with integer effective capacities. Turning to the choice of applicant-specific recovery permissions before costs are reported, we show that a common appended recovery pool gives diminishing returns, whereas overlapping profiles can conceal strictly joint value. When firm capacity accommodates all but one workload and one recovery award completes the cohort, an exact financial frontier permits optimal permission selection by virtual-cost distributions, although capacity expansion can reverse the preferred recipient. A sharp deletion-loss bound limits globally indispensable permissions to 19 at a 95% target, even though minimum satisfactory menus can be arbitrarily large. In the unchanged 27-setting block design, minimum richer menus repair all 16 failed unit restrictions: five need one paired permission and eleven need two, with every displayed retained permission necessary within its selected menu. Separate overlapping-menu experiments distinguish financial failure from unsuccessful certification.

detail.abstract: In stochastic user equilibrium (SUE) traffic assignment with fixed path sets and a logit route choice model, we derive bounds on the distance between a given feasible solution and the equilibrium solution. The intent is to provide guidance on termination criteria to reduce run times, which is important because the traffic assignment problem is often a subproblem of a more complex bi-level optimization. Our approach is based on the partial linearization of the SUE objective and provides upper bounds on differences in both aggregate metrics like total system travel time (TSTT) and disaggregate metrics such as link flows and path flows. We demonstrate that the derived path flow, link flow, link cost, and TSTT bounds are tight and cannot be further improved by a fixed factor without additional restrictions on the network topology or problem instance. Results on four city-level networks indicate that, at a relative gap of 10⁻⁶, the bounds guarantee that the path flows, link flows, link costs, and TSTT are all within 0.1% of their equilibrium values for a logit dispersion parameter of 0.5, and within 1% for a dispersion parameter of 1.5. Furthermore, we show the error bounds converge to zero at least as fast as the path flows converge in the underlying algorithm used to solve for SUE. We demonstrate the practical utility of the derived bounds in a network design problem to minimize a weighted sum of TSTT and construction cost. Using a local search on the Chicago Sketch network, we show that the bounds allow 96% of the candidate designs to be rejected before their traffic assignment is solved to high accuracy, resulting in a 45% reduction in computation time compared with not using them.

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming marketing practices through advanced data analysis and predictive capabilities. This paper examines AI driven marketing, focusing on customer behavior analysis and predictive marketing. It explores how AI technologies help businesses understand customer preferences, identify purchasing patterns, and anticipate future customer actions. The study discusses applications such as customer segmentation, recommendation systems, sentiment analysis, customer churn prediction, and customer lifetime value estimation. It also examines AI applications across commerce, banking, healthcare, travel, hospitality, and social media marketing. The paper highlights potential benefits, including personalization, improved decision making, marketing efficiency, customer retention, and demand forecasting. However, effective implementation requires attention to data quality, privacy, algorithmic bias, implementation costs, and technical expertise. Ethical considerations, including transparency, consent, fairness, security, and human oversight, remain essential for responsible AI adoption. The paper follows a conceptual approach based on secondary literature. It concludes that AI can strengthen marketing effectiveness by integrating customer insights with predictive capabilities. Successful implementation requires collaboration between human marketers and AI technologies. This balanced approach can support customer relationships, informed decisions, and sustainable marketing performance.

detail.abstract: Electronic reporting rules determine the form in which corporate disclosures enter official records and become available for analysis. Their operation raises a legal question about the evidential significance of technical acceptance: which aspects of compliance can an automated result establish, and who remains responsible for the judgments it leaves unresolved? This article develops a functional comparison of the European Single Electronic Format, the European Single Access Point and the United States EDGAR system. It examines admission, classification, temporal ordering and circulation through legislation, implementing measures and filing instructions. The comparison distinguishes the existing ESEF format regime and operational EDGAR system from the prospective ESAP access infrastructure. It shows how a change in validation severity can obstruct submission, how taxonomy extensions require interpretive choices, and how correction metadata affects the reconstruction of a disclosure history. Technical acceptance supplies evidence of the checks performed on a particular submission; its legal significance depends on the governing rules and the reliability of that record. The article proposes an allocation of responsibility in which issuers retain responsibility for their disclosures, operators explain the constraints they administer, and regulators specify the consequences of technical events. Public specifications, proportionate rejection rules and accessible correction procedures should support that allocation. The resulting framework connects the design of reporting infrastructure to the legal duties and evidential uses that justify it.

detail.abstract: Sustainability transitions scholarship has developed two largely parallel analytical vocabularies: one explaining how incumbent regimes become locked in, the other how niche actors respond. This paper connects them through a framework of regime lock-in profilestrategy alignment. Nested within the Multi-Level Perspective, it characterizes regime lock-ins by tractability, materiality, coordination requirement, and coupling intensity, with regime coherence as a context-level modifier; and then introduces bypass-repurpose-weaken (BRW) typology that classifies niche strategies by the functional mechanism through which they engage regime lock-ins based on their structural profiles. A six-step operational protocol is further proposed, and the framework's central proposition is empirically illustrated through an embedded case study of Roam, an electric motorcycle manufacturer in Kenya's boda boda sector. The case provides pattern-consistent support for the proposition: bypass clusters around material, tractable lock-ins; weaken around less material, tractable lock-ins; and repurpose where existing regime elements remain redirectable. The resulting pathway is characterised as bounded leapfrogging. Portability across regime configurations is specified analytically, while comparative testing remains necessary before prescriptive claims can be validated.

detail.abstract: The McKinsey Global Institute (MGI) estimates that, by 2035, automation could reduce U.S. labor demand by about a fifth of current work hours, while broader growth creates more jobs than automation removes. About 11 million workers may need to change occupations in the next decade. Colleges and universities plan programs years ahead, so they need to know what this scenario means for the programs they offer and the places they serve. We translate the MGI scenario into estimates for 830 detailed occupations, 1,432 academic program families at four award levels, and 530 metropolitan and nonmetropolitan areas. A task-level model of AI adoption, built from language-model exposure, observed AI success and review time, the cost of errors and governance, distributes MGI's totals across occupations. We also report the model's independent estimate and explain where and why it differs from MGI. Almost no occupation disappears: one falls by more than half and 62 fall by 20-50%. About 9.5 million jobs are in occupations that decline, almost half of them in office and administrative support. Program risk sits below the bachelor's degree. About 8% of certificate and 7% of associate completions are in programs whose graduates' occupations shrink by 10% or more, while 48% of certificates and 32% of associate degrees are in programs whose fields grow by 10% or more. At the bachelor's and graduate levels demand is broadly stable, but AI is expected to adopt or augment more than half of graduates' work hours, so the task is curriculum reinvention rather than closure. The need to change jobs is greatest in rural, agricultural and lower-wage areas; the wages at stake are greatest in high-wage hubs. We set out a roadmap for investment, reinvention, consolidation and review.

detail.abstract: Family enterprises in Africa and the Gulf are entering a period of generational transfer, yet the ways value is lost during that transfer are rarely named together. This paper introduces the idea of succession leakage: the gradual or sudden loss of economic, relational and institutional value that occurs because a transition was unplanned, poorly planned or planned in isolation. It proposes a taxonomy of eight leakage channels, describes the early signs of each, and sets out five propositions for empirical testing. It uses two recent regulatory developments, Kenya's Trust Administration Act, 2026 and the Dubai International Financial Centre's family-wealth framework, to show how legal change can turn a dormant weakness into an immediate one. The paper is conceptual. It reports no empirical results and does not claim that any diagnostic instrument has been validated. Its aim is to give researchers and practitioners a shared vocabulary and a testable research agenda.

detail.abstract: Honest difference-indifferences methods judge how far parallel trends may fail after treatment by how far it failed before treatment, as shown by placebo estimates. When the design adjusts for covariates, the placebo estimates are adjusted too. We show that this benchmark is valid only if the covariates are measured before the earliest placebo window. A covariate measured later already reflects shocks to the outcome during the placebo period, so adjusting for it hides part of the pre-trend. The placebos then look flatter than the true trend and the resulting confidence sets are too narrow. When the covariate is also observed at an early date, the distortion can be estimated and tested. Of 90 recent published studies that adjust for time-varying covariates, 77 measure at least one covariate too late.

detail.abstract: Stronger positive externalities can lead to more severe overinvestment in sectors experiencing an innovation boom. We develop a model with pioneering cases, irreversible capital, subsequent incremental innovation, loan pricing, and competition among local governments for projects to explain this counterintuitive relationship. The diffusion of successful cases can convey valuable information while amplifying selection neglect; technological diffusion lowers replication costs and allows followers to profit through business stealing; credit and local bidding further stimulate construction. Each channel has a parameter region in which it strictly increases overinvestment. Even with entirely correct beliefs, a rise in the true external value of knowledge can make market investment expand faster than socially optimal investment. We derive an investment criterion at finite parameter values: the difference between locally captured average knowledge benefits per project and the nationwide marginal knowledge contribution, together with business stealing and belief distortions, determines the boundary between underinvestment and overinvestment. The criterion accommodates resource opportunity costs that rise with expansion. When knowledge continues to grow, a local capture share above the investment elasticity of knowledge output implies that higher external value increases excess investment and allocative loss. Interactions also matter. Lower replication costs amplify the investment effects of optimism and project bidding and bring forward the onset of overinvestment. Near the investment boundary, the joint allocative loss exceeds the sum of the losses from the three channels acting separately. The policy results distinguish optimal total support for innovation from additional central intervention in local competition: total support can rise even as stronger central offsets become necessary. Correcting subsequent entry also preserves the informational value of pioneering activity, allowing support for exploration and restraints on expansion to complement one another. The direction of industrial policy therefore depends on the net social contribution of additional investment and the investment response it induces.

detail.abstract: Starting from legitimate property rights and voluntary exchange, this paper compares a regime that protects existing land-use rights with specific regimes that permit nonconsensual reassignment of rights. It establishes two potential advantages of the former in coordinating externalities. First, when both regimes can attain the ideal maximum of resource allocation efficiency, the regime protecting existing rights achieves the same efficiency while respecting authorization and voluntary consent throughout the formation, enforcement, and adjustment of rights. Second, in separate models of irreversible investment, transaction costs, and private information, it strictly reduces efficiency losses under the stated conditions while retaining its advantage in rights protection, given common technologies, information, and contractual instruments. The unifying mechanism is the continued effectiveness ex post of coordination arrangements voluntarily established ex ante: use caps constrain additional investment, continuing permits save repeated coordination costs, and ex ante contingent contracts preserve information-revelation and trading arrangements. The investment model shows that negotiable use caps implement the first best and quantifies the construction and location losses caused by administrative permit expansion. A fiscal model of permit reissuance further derives revocation decisions and their consequences from government revenue maximization, jointly endogenizing reassignment and resource losses in the transactioncost and information branches. Contract redesign identifies the scope of these comparisons. Together, the two sets of results show that, in the institutional environments considered here, protecting existing rights is compatible with maximum efficiency and can also yield efficiency advantages in the presence of frictions.

detail.abstract: This paper establishes two connected propositions under zero transaction costs and complete contracts. First, firms can create value by implementing production plans and organizing complementary inputs; positive transaction costs are not a necessary condition for their existence. Project surplus can support voluntary firm formation, a model of productive inputs yields a threshold for operation at a positive scale, and an occupational choice model further establishes a competitive equilibrium with a positive mass of firms. These two propositions organize the paper. The subsequent analysis distinguishes asset ownership, effective control, and the firm, and shows how complete contracts can replicate dynamic production policies, clarifying the conditions under which each result applies.

detail.abstract: What happens to price discovery when a growing share of the traders in a market are autonomous language-model agents? We build an event-sourced continuous double-auction exchange with exact accounting, a latent dividend process that separates fundamental value from public value and transaction price, seven calibrated classical trader types, and an adapter that lets a language model trade from a canonical snapshot through a strictly validated JSON action. We then run randomized, matched-seed experiments in which 0 to 100 percent of trader slots are exogenously assigned to a small reasoning model (gpt-5.4-nano), holding fundamentals, news, endowments, latencies and information sets fixed, with a pre-registered analysis plan, seven matched seeds per live cell and thirty per classical cell. A stylized model with correlated signal errors predicts that a shared model degrades informativeness, raises order-flow correlation and amplifies leverage-driven spirals, and that model diversity restores informativeness. The simulator confirms the predictions on coordination and diversity and rejects them on prices: raising the LLM share tightens quoted spreads from 19 to 6 basis points, multiplies depth by seven, cuts price impact by 60 percent and leaves the pricing error unchanged, while the market absorbs latent information more slowly and returns become predictable (variance ratio 2.1, lag-one autocorrelation 0.32 at full penetration). No bubble or crash appears in 112 live runs, and with leveraged traders present the LLM agents halve the pricing error and remove the bubble episodes the leverage creates. Prompt diversity and a two-model mix lower coordination and shorten absorption at a liquidity cost; a communication channel and memory raise coordination and pricing error slightly. The unifying mechanism is patient, public-value-anchored liquidity provision by agents who act infrequently. All results are causal statements about the simulator, reproducible from a one-command replication package; the Anthropic cells of the design are implemented but could not be run.

detail.abstract: For two centuries, economics has split its assumptions about "man" into the rational-agent tradition and behavioral economics, and the two together have left one question unanswered: where do preferences come from. This paper proposes a third path: the Desiring-Person Axiom — humans have desires; desires are structured into three layers and six slots (subsistence/belonging/meaning × defense/offense); slot dominance is modulated by the institutional-trust environment. From this single axiom, rational behavior emerges as the limit of a stable, high-trust environment (covering the rational agent), and behavioral deviations emerge as products of the decoding layer under persistent uncertainty (covering the irrational agent). The axiom thereby acquires two properties that neither camp has: coverage and falsifiability. The evidence is layered. At the macro level, three stations of real data support the axiom's predictions (149-country happiness cross-section with subsistence as the dominant peak; 175-country governmentexpenditure response, p=0.006; a 38-observation event panel with double significance for persistent shocks). At the individual level, HFCS Italian household data (22,300 observations) show that the offense– defense structure obeys the axiom (north–south trust gradient p<0.0001), and further reveal a three-layer isomorphism chain: firms (S&P 500 capability accumulation × market-value premium, Tobin's Q 1.58 vs 0.69), individuals (nonlinear financial-asset growth, capability p=0.0024), and nations (institutional– meaning crystallization × GDP resilience p=0.0015, plus monetary reach ρ=+0.261) — high-crystallization actors consistently "defend capability, not stock." The paper proposes a three-layer × offense–defense-axis abstraction of individual crystallization (subsistence → belonging → meaning, with institutional crystallization cutting across along the offense– defense axis) and a reproducible measurement protocol (zero-application data, minimal measurement, dual-definition robustness, six attack-point defenses fully disclosed), and explicitly separates education (capability boundary) from meaning (direction of desire): education is a proxy for capability, not for meaning. Three-layer isomorphism receives strong consistent support (criteria 1-3 and 5 fully satisfied; criterion 4, cross-layer parameter comparability, partially satisfied and listed as an extension); a unified isomorphism equation is listed as an extension.

detail.abstract: This paper forges the proposition that "prices and markets mutually constitute each other" into a testable theoretical system. On the basis of four axioms (dispersed evaluation, dispersed knowledge, freedom of choice, and scarcity), the paper proves three theorems: (i) the Emergence Theorem-prices are an emergent property of the interaction of all agents, and there exists no price-setter; (ii) the Dissolution Theorem-replacing prices with a command system is not an intervention into the market but the dissolution of the market; prices can only be driven out, never abolished; (iii) the Incomputability Theorem-the objective function of a planning system does not exist under the given axioms, let alone is computable. Analytically, the paper presents three evolutionary-game models of the Emergence Theorem (convention emergence, scarcity tracking, non-authorship) and shows that emergent prices converge to Walrasian prices in the large-population limit, with deviations attributable to trading institutions rather than to any pricing agent. Empirically, 600 multi-institution, multi-seed simulations verify two crossinstitutional invariants (non-authorship and a monotone scarcity trend) and yield a third result: the price level as an "institutional fingerprint." The econometric section provides the first systematic test of the Dissolution Theorem's four empirical footprints: a daily break-point event study of Argentina's foreign-exchange controls (break t =-54.7 at the repeal of the cepo); the Ilzetzki-Reinhart-Rogoff full panel of parallel-market existence across 179 countries (1946-2019), whose institution-group regressions show existence probabilities rising monotonically with the intensity of administrative control (+16 pp for crawling bands, +37 pp for freely falling, with freely floating as an insignificant negative control); and a three-country premium panel (Argentina, Algeria, Iraq) in which countries carrying nearly identical regime labels exhibit a nearly sixfold premium gap-the premium tracks the intensity of administrative rationing, not the nominal regime. The philosophical harvest, stated conservatively, comprises two corollaries: the individual is the only acting subject (E1), and there exists no "end of society itself" superior to the welfare of individuals (E2).

detail.abstract: The convergence of Nash equilibria of large N-player games to mean field game equilibria has been extensively studied over the past decade, particularly for finite horizon games. For infinite horizon ergodic games, however, this convergence problem remains less well understood and is known to fail in general. In this paper, we address the question for open-loop equilibria in the displacement monotone setting and derive explicit convergence rates. Specifically, we study ergodic games with drift and volatility control, as well as common noise, without requiring time-homogeneous coefficients. Our approach is based on a version of the Pontryagin maximum principle adapted for ergodic control problems and the resulting infinite horizon McKean-Vlasov Forward Backward Stochastic Differential Equations (FBSDEs), for which we prove well-posedness. Solutions to these FBSDEs are shown to correspond to particular equilibria of feedback nature, for which we prove quantitative convergence using uniform in time propagation of chaos estimates. In contrast to the finite horizon setting, the particular equilibria found using FBSDEs need not be unique, and we analyze situations when the convergence result can be extended for general equilibria.

detail.title: Bounded Agency: A Relational Theory of Expected-State Formation, Recursive Load, and Constrained Action

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: This paper develops a theory of bounded agency: an account of how an agent forms expectations about the world, distinguishes what it wants from what is the case, allocates a finite capacity, holds itself together under the internal cost of doing so, and acts into a field that affords, resists, or distorts the conversion of its effort into effect. The central claim is that the realized effect of an agent is not a property the agent carries, but a joint product of its available capacity, the internal load it bears, the efficiency with which capacity reaches the world, and the alignment between its aim and the field's structure. The theory is relational without being vague: it distinguishes constitution from mere influence, and it specifies four structural features by which a constitutively held property can in principle be told apart from a merely influenced one. The account is designed to generate falsifiable claims rather than to function as an interpretive frame, and it is held to an explicit validation discipline that separates reasoned proposals from verified results. The theory is a structural account of agency, not a measure of human worth, competence, or entitlement. It admits several applications, among them interpersonal dynamics, social simulation, and designed agents, and is identified with none of them.

detail.abstract: Whether financial leverage raises or lowers the stock returns demanded by investors remains an open empirical question, and the answer may be highly industry-specific. This paper examines the relation between leverage and realized stock returns among the A-share listed automobile manufacturers of China, exploiting a decade in which the industry was split by the transition from internal combustion engines to new energy vehicles. Using an unbalanced panel of 21 firms over 2015-2024, with 185 firm-year observations, pooled panel regressions with year fixed effects and firm-clustered standard errors are estimated for the full sample and for three groups defined by business model: new energy vehicle makers, traditional passenger vehicle makers, and commercial vehicle makers. The full-sample association is weakly positive, a marginally significant coefficient of 0.44 on total leverage that masks substantial heterogeneity. Commercial vehicle makers exhibit a strongly positive leverage-return relation, whereas the relation for traditional passenger vehicle makers is negative and indistinguishable from zero, and the two slopes differ significantly. The contrast between new energy and traditional passenger makers is not statistically significant, a result attributable to the small size of the new energy subsample. The findings indicate that leverage carries distinct risk and distress information across business models within a single industry, and that pooled estimates of the leverage premium can conceal as much as they reveal.

detail.abstract: Over the past six years, research on highperformance public Layer-1 blockchains has reported throughput gains of up to two orders of magnitude. However, the interpretability and comparability of these claims remain limited by insufficient reporting and substantial reliance on secondary sources. We screened 810 records, audited 299 published performance claims, and constructed a 200-row matrix linking identified performance-enhancement mechanisms to their documented costs. First, only 14 of 92 numerical throughput claims had a verifiable validator count in the same passage as the reported figure; six of these appeared in papers authored by system developers. Second, of the 299 audited performance claims, 87 came from secondary sources, such as other research articles or vendor materials, rather than the measurements reported by the papers citing them. Lastly, 30 of the 200 costs are paid in a different layer of the stack from the one that earns the benefit, 37 rest on production measurement, and the two systems with the largest deployment throughput have no archival description of their core mechanisms. We argue that a key limitation is the evaluation of individual mechanisms in isolation, despite their deployment as interconnected stacks. We propose a seven-field Performance Claim Card, an attribution rule for comparison tables, evidence grading as a reporting norm, and a distinction between mechanism evaluation and stack evaluation that venues can enforce through artifact review.

title: Do Carbon Prices Reduce Emissions? Global Evidence from Thirty Years of Carbon Taxes and Markets using Staggered Difference-in-Differences

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates whether the adoption of explicit carbon prices-taxes and emissions trading systems-has reduced CO 2 emissions. It uses a panel of 143 countries over 1985-2022, 41 of which adopt a price with significant coverage, and combines data from the Global Carbon Budget with the World Carbon Pricing Database. Modern staggered differencein-differences estimators (Callaway-Sant'Anna, Sun-Abraham, imputation), synthetic control and SDID are applied. The two-way fixed effects estimator implies an effect on per capita emissions of-38.8 log points, and the heterogeneity-robust estimators about-18 points over the first eleven years. However, all of them reveal pronounced pre-trends: adopters were already reducing their relative emissions by almost 2% per year before adopting. The TWFE bias from comparisons across cohorts is of second order; the main problem is selection on trends. With comparable controls and country-specific trends-a specification that passes a temporal placebo test that the conventional one fails-the average effect shrinks to between-2.5 and +9 log points, with no statistical significance. No gradient of the effects with the effective carbon price is detected, although this estimate is imprecise. The reductions that persist are concentrated in the 2005 EU ETS cohort and coincide with the fall in GDP associated with the 2008-2013 crisis. By contrast, adoption is robustly associated with an increase of about 2 percentage points in the share of renewables, and an aggregate indicator based on consumption-based emissions does not show the pattern that substantial carbon leakage would predict, although its scope is limited. The results suggest that the aggregate crosscountry evidence on the effectiveness of carbon pricing is considerably more fragile than is usually acknowledged.

detail.abstract: When should a regulator require an established platform to interoperate with its rivals? We study the date of a permanent interoperability mandate in a finite-horizon duopoly with direct network effects, persistent user bases, forward-looking prices, and an incumbent that can install the standard voluntarily in any period. The welfare gain from advancing the mandate by one period equals the value of cross-network access if the two networks were of equal size, minus a penalty proportional to the square of the incumbent's initial lead, minus the per-period user cost of the technology. Pricing, reallocation and persistence effects enter at second order in the ratio of network benefits to product differentiation; across 3,471 economies in which the equilibrium conditions hold they never exceed 5 percent of the gain, and a rule that ignores them selects the welfare-maximizing deadline in 3,449 of them. When the net gain from advancing changes sign once over time, the optimal deadline is the first date at which it is positive; to first order, this is the first date at which the product of the two networks' sizes is large enough for the access gain to cover the user cost. Interior deadlines arise in growing markets, mature symmetric markets call for an immediate mandate or none, and a larger incumbent lead delays the welfare-optimal date. Consumers favor earlier mandates than the regulator whenever the user cost exceeds the revenue gain that compatibility gives the platforms. An announced deadline raises acquisition prices before compliance. In the numerical benchmark, a mandate one period too early forgoes 2 percent of the mandate's value and one period too late 7 percent.

detail.abstract: Hyperscale compute is expanding alongside rapid urbanization, yet city planning still treats data centers as isolated, power-hungry industrial liabilities whose waste heat is simply dumped into the atmosphere. Project Apiary presents a conceptual architecture-the "Hive City"-that reframes subterranean high-density compute as a metabolic asset. Urban space is organized into three tiers: Subterranean Compute Vaults, a surface Mandala-Grid of walkable superblocks, and a Honeycomb Agricultural Canopy. Low-grade heat from liquid-cooled servers feeds year-round food production and district heating; the cooled fluid returns to the bedrock vaults. This paper outlines the spatial, thermal, economic and governance principles of the model. It is offered as a theoretical framework that relies only on existing or near-future technology; it is not a validated design, engineering specification, or construction blueprint. The paper closes with an explicit list of open questions for others to examine, challenge or build upon.

detail.abstract: Purpose-This study examines how employees of a public tertiary hospital appraise their work demands and reward system, which motivators they value, and whether they believe motivation improves their performance. Design/methodology/approach-A stratified cross-sectional survey of 74 employees (response rate 86%) from seven departments of Federal Medical Centre, Ebute-Metta, Lagos, Nigeria, analysed descriptively with 95% confidence intervals; a previously reported correlation is reexamined. Findings-Seventy-three per cent of respondents were dissatisfied with the hospital's motivational packages, 72% disagreed that staff were adequately motivated, and 68% disliked their workload. Every respondent valued achievement, advancement and growth, and 96% endorsed pay and promotion as motivators. Views on leadership communication, training and recognition were more divided. The very strong reported correlations between motivation and perceived performance (ρ = 0.86-0.92) reflect overlapping measures, not a performance effect. Research limitations/implications-Evidence is from one site, is self-reported and cross-sectional, and was collected with an unvalidated instrument; performance was not measured independently. Practical implications-Where pay and promotion are set nationally, hospital managers can act on how fairly and transparently rewards are administered, how workload is allocated, and how leaders communicate and provide development opportunities. Performance management should rely on independent indicators rather than on perceptions of motivation's effects. Originality/value-The study provides multi-occupational evidence from a Nigerian public hospital that employees value intrinsic and extrinsic rewards together, and it identifies a gap between the rewards employees value most and the levers hospital managers control.

detail.abstract: Despite extensive policy efforts to reduce U.S. residential CO2 emissions, identifying the most effective interventions remains challenging. We apply a machine learning-based approach to detect structural breaks in residential CO2 emissions from 1998 to 2019. This method extends reverse-causal techniques by detecting both trend and step breaks to identify gradual emission reductions. The resulting breaks in trends reveal the abnormal periods of emission changes, which can be interpreted as agnostically detected heterogeneous time-varying treatment effects in a difference-indifferences framework. We then address the challenge of identifying the potential causes of the changes by employing two complementary approaches: (i) linking detected break dates to the Database of State Incentives for Renewables and Efficiency (DSIRE) and (ii) assessing the potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) for event attribution. Our findings reveal significant reductions in residential CO2 emissions, with both database-driven and LLMbased attribution suggesting that rebate programs, tax incentives, and building energy codes have been the most effective policy types.

detail.abstract: This study audits twelve legacy Rule 605 reports from Citadel Securities and Virtu for January-June 2026. It compares a spread-specific sample with one requiring exact price-class reconciliation and measures how that screen changes volume, composition, and spread comparisons. In January, price-class deficits totaling 6,067 reported shares occur in Citadel market-order cells representing 7.627 billion executed shares. Exact reconciliation removes 56.84% of that venue family's marketorder exposure, raises its mean effective spread from $0.012876 to $0.016207 per share, and reduces Virtu's matched-volume coverage from 99.89% to 43.61%. These changes measure the effects of the analyst's selection rule; they do not estimate missing trades or investor losses. The six-month audit also examines what reported outside-quote incidence establishes about an unobserved customer group. Established counting bounds, explicit example allocations, and a minimum group-size threshold specify what aggregate rates can certify. A separate assumption about unclassified shares distinguishes uncertainty about a small accounting gap from the much larger uncertainty about customer membership. The contribution is a reproducible account of selection amplification and disclosure limits. It offers no new general identification theorem or causal finding against either institution.

detail.abstract: As robotics and artificial intelligence advance rapidly, automation-related policies have gained prominence in industrialized economies. Based on a growth model with capital-embodied technical change, this study investigates the effects of three distinct subsidy instruments: subsidies for intermediate goods, subsidies for automation, and subsidies for vertical innovation. Theoretical analysis reveals that while intermediate-good and automation subsidies promote long-run growth, innovation subsidies hinder it by crowding out automation. Calibrated to US data, our quantitative analysis shows that although innovation subsidies are detrimental to long-run growth, they generate a positive effect in the short run. We further compare the steady-state and transitional welfare effects, finding that the policy implications for automation and innovation subsidies shift when transition dynamics are considered, whereas the implications for intermediate-good subsidies remain unchanged. Finally, we characterize the dynamically optimal policy mix required to replicate the first-best outcome, demonstrating that the welfare loss from implementing the constrained long-run optimal policy is non negligible. These results highlight the critical importance of transition dynamics in the design of optimal policy.

detail.abstract:
We test whether a score derived only from the scientific literature improves
equity portfolios that other people chose. The score uses no prices,
fundamentals or analyst data. No input, embedding model, prediction or company
description used in the evaluation draws on papers or filings dated after it.

Each quarter from March 2020 to October 2026 we examine the arXiv 
papers available at that date, select groups of papers with a proprietary
method, and score US-listed companies by how closely the business section of
their latest 10-K matches the existing and expected discoveries in those groups. We then re-weight, by
rank of that score, the reported long US equity holdings of every 13F filer
that meets fixed data rules: 1,171 managers, including asset managers, pension
funds, banks, insurers and hedge funds. Each tilt keeps the manager's own
holdings and prices; only the weights change, and only at report dates. The
tilt's one parameter, a similarity threshold, is chosen walk-forward from past
results.

Over 26 quarters, from March 2020 to October 2026, the tilt adds
**+1.31 percentage points a year** to the average manager's own book. Random
orderings of the same holdings, put through the same procedure, add +0.33
(z = 8.0; no draw of 1,000 reaches the observed value). The tilt improves 85%
of the books and beats random orderings at p < 0.05 for 458 managers. The active return leans
toward growth; after market, value and size factors the pooled alpha is
+0.59 pp a year (t = 2.3). On the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100, against the real
index funds, the tilt adds +2.01 and +2.69 pp a year, and +1.16 and +1.95 after
style. A forward test on holdings and prices that do not yet exist has been
registered (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23692720).

detail.abstract: Lifecycle consumption and portfolio decisions involve many interrelated factors, including financial market uncertainty, health risks, and medical expenditures, making joint optimization computationally challenging. To address this, we develop a reinforcement learning (RL) framework based on proximal policy optimization (PPO) for high-dimensional life cycle problems. To accommodate the age-dependent structure of life cycle problems and the intra-period sequencing of financial decisions, we derive a finite-horizon policy-improvement lower bound, construct a trajectory-weighted empirical objective, and develop a sequential conditional policy architecture with blockwise updates. To strengthen portfolio learning, we introduce a portfolio-specific conditional advantage estimator. Theoretical analysis establishes first-order stationarity results and characterizes the effect of critic approximation error. We then apply the framework to a multi-asset life cycle model with variable annuities and health-dependent medical expenditures, using health-state transition probabilities estimated from longitudinal data from the Health and Retirement Study (HRS). In a lower-dimensional setting where dynamic programming (DP) is computationally feasible, numerical experiments show that the proposed framework closely reproduces the DP solutions, while the portfolio-specific estimator further improves investment policy accuracy. In a richer setting, we examine how disability-related medical expenditures and expanded diversification opportunities affect life cycle consumption, portfolio allocation, and liquid-wealth decumulation.

detail.abstract: A Chinese given name is built from characters with everyday meanings, so a buyer can read it for the character of the person who carries it. We measure the trust a buyer reads into the given names of the closing agents of a nationwide brokerage platform, taking the construct from the warmth-and-competence framework of social cognition and reading it two ways, with a hand-coded dictionary of the two dimensions and with a generative AI model asked the same question about the characters alone, and we price it on 1.8 million second-hand home sales across China. A closing agent with a trustworthy name gives up a deep discount less often: by four and a half percent of the base rate across listings, by a third within the same home sold twice, and by more than half within the same household buying twice. The name does not forecast how many deals the agent closes or whether she is promoted, so the market prices a cue that carries no information about her performance, the case of inaccurate statistical discrimination. Two designs then isolate the step the transaction record cannot show. An agent-based simulation with generative AI models rebuilds the closing table with the home, the script and every word of the price defense held fixed while only the agent's name changes: the simulated buyer trusts the same defense more and demands a smaller concession, and never mentions the name in the reason she gives. A within-person experiment puts the same manipulation to human buyers, each rating trusted and untrusted names side by side on the same listing: the name raises the belief that the agent is reliable, and the concession follows that belief. The paper brings the money-doctor mechanism of the finance of trust to a single named counterparty, whose trust was set by her parents' naming fashion decades before the sale.

detail.abstract: What would a stock portfolio look like if no rule were allowed to read a price? We built one from published accounts alone (healthy firms, investing at a normal pace, ranked by the cash they generate) and froze its rules. Its first backtest beat the S&P 500 in four savings plans out of five. It was wrong: every company in its price file had survived. Re-tested on survivorship-free US data from July 1999 to May 2026, the strategy earns 15.9% a year after costs against 8.5% for the S&P 500, yet nearly all of its advantage arrived in two bursts, after the market lows of 2002 and 2009. Its picks beat all ten random portfolios drawn from the same candidates before 2011 and eight of ten after, so the picking did not break; the pond did. In published accounts, small firms stopped out-growing large ones, fewer stayed healthy, and the market began to reward holding winners. A last test held a surprise: July, the formation month fixed before any test, was the luckiest of the four quarterly months; averaged over them, the strategy earns about 13% a year. Thirty-nine pre-declared variants, two of them borrowed from game theory, fail to improve both periods. We report all of about eighty configurations and a forward test frozen in October 2026.

detail.abstract: For a prescribed spacetime metric, testing whether its Einstein stress tensor satisfies the weak or null energy condition admits a convex formulation with explicit separating certificates. Using the S-lemma, both conditions become one-parameter linear matrix inequalities at each event, valid for all Hawking–Ellis types; the dual cone consists of causal mixtures, so every violation carries a certificate and a causal witness direction. Adding covariant conservation on the fixed background as a linear constraint, a weak-duality construction supplies a verified numerical lower bound on the distance from the target to the nearest conserved, WEC-admissible tensor field, closely approached by a near-feasible candidate from Dykstra’s projections. This quantifies tensor mismatch under necessary admissibility conditions; it does not construct a matter model or a new geometry. We compute Alcubierre and Natário stress tensors with an Einstein-tensor solver validated against closed forms, the momentum constraint (to 5 × 10⁻¹⁶), an independent finite-difference route and the contracted Bianchi identity. Both drives lie at a relative distance of 0.72 to 0.73 from the WEC cone; with covariant conservation the distance is about 0.77 for Alcubierre (0.765 to 0.769 across three grids and two domain sizes) and 0.773 to 0.782 for Natário, decreasing under refinement, each given by a verified numerical lower bound that a near-feasible field approaches to about 10⁻⁹. We prove that whenever the stress tensor is a first-order time–space field plus a second-order remainder, a hypothesis both drives satisfy exactly, the slow-bubble distance tends to 1/√2. The witness directions are ultrarelativistic and point along the energy flux, and the Eulerian cell test common in optimization codes measures the violation at about 1% of its size. We then bound the positive energy needed to make the target admissible without changing its momentum density. The answer depends on the matter added. Exact cell-wise lower bounds, whose slow-bubble asymptotics are 2∫|S|dV for Eulerian dust and ∫|S|dV for matter obeying the dominant energy condition, are attained for dust and bracketed to within 1.5% for DEC matter, while matter obeying only the WEC can approach the drive’s own negative energy at the cost of divergent pressure. These corrections are pointwise and not conserved. For a 100 m Alcubierre bubble at 0.1c the dust and DEC corrections are 4.5 × 10²⁸ and 2.3 × 10²⁸ kg of equivalent massenergy, against a drive energy of −3.0 × 10²⁶ kg. Finally, applied to the positive-energy warp shell of Fuchs et al., rebuilt from its public source, the method confirms that the null, weak, strong and dominant conditions hold for every observer at the published shift amplitude of 0.02. It also shows that all four fail together at a critical amplitude of 0.0304, where the null constraint of energy plus pressure against twice the momentum density binds in the shell’s equatorial plane.

detail.abstract: Legal responses to workplace exhaustion increasingly oblige or reward institutions that listen to the people they employ: psychosocial risk assessments, occupational health units, confidential counselling, periodic examinations. Every act of listening produces a record, and the law has said little about what that record may become. This article asks what limits human dignity places on what an employing institution may remember about exhaustion, and who should control that memory. The method is doctrinal and functional-comparative. It examines Brazil (CNJ Resolution 207/2015, the NR-1 psychosocial-risk rules and their 2026 judicial suspension, the LGPD and the Federal Supreme Court's treatment of forgetting), Germany, England and Wales, and the European data-protection and human-rights overlay (GDPR Article 88, CJEU C-34/21 and C-65/23, Bărbulescu, S. and Marper). The Brazilian novel O Prédio que Aprendeu a Escutar, whose courthouse listens without knowing how to forget, serves as an interpretive case and is not offered as evidence. The article advances an interpretive and normative thesis, not an empirical finding: the regimes examined treat listening as intake and memory as accumulation, and lack a doctrine of the life of the record. Dignity, read through the disclosure dilemma that listening creates, supports an asymmetry in institutional memory: durable and aggregate as to working conditions, purpose-bound, contestable and person-controlled as to individual disclosures of suffering. The strongest objection, that memory is what lets workers prove employer notice, narrows the thesis but does not defeat it. Implications for rule design in judiciaries and other public employers are drawn from the analysis, and the conditions under which the thesis would fail are specified.

detail.abstract:
When machines can lead the prayer, play the lover and carry out the crime, who answers for what they do? The Forbidden follows artificial intelligence and robotics into the four domains that societies have always set apart: the sacred, the intimate, the criminal and the dead. It argues that in each, the machine can perform the act but cannot carry what gives the act its meaning. A machine can recite a prayer but cannot pray as a being that will die. It can offer devotion but not love that could have been refused. It can do the work of a criminal crew but cannot have a guilty mind. It can speak in a dead person’s voice but cannot live a life that ends.

The book draws on the rulings of six faiths, criminal and civil law in several jurisdictions, and recent research on companion AI, automated crime, digital afterlives, addictive design and neurotechnology. It applies the series’ framework of three roads to each domain. On the Owners’ Road, companies set the lines. On the State’s Road, governments set them. On the Shared Road, the people who must live within the lines draw them. Four models are built from published data and tested against figures they were not built from, and each test changed the text:

  • the share of the fall in fertility that comes from fewer partnerships, in Japan and England and Wales;
  • the stage at which crimes go unsolved, using police outcome data;
  • when the dead will outnumber the living among users of an online service;
  • how far the revenue of attention-holding products depends on their heaviest users.

The book also sets out the fiction that imagined each technology before it was built, from Pygmalion to Her. It argues that such fiction has often become a specification for the builders, who took the wish and left the warning. It closes with eight institutional proposals, each extending an existing rule to the machines:

  • disclosure;
  • user ownership of companion data;
  • design limits on addictive products;
  • registration and strict liability for capable machines;
  • judicial control of machine records;
  • consent in life for posthumous likenesses;
  • faith communities’ control of their own tools;
  • absolute protection of children.

Each chapter states the strongest objection to its own argument and the observations that would show it wrong.

The Forbidden is Book 6 of The Next Human Epoch and the third book of Part 2. It is available open access at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23708297.

detail.abstract: The iShares Core U.S. Aggregate Bond ETF and the Vanguard Total Bond Market Index Fund hold similar US investment-grade bonds, yet in their SEC filings one reports its interest-rate sensitivity as positive and the other as negative. For a hypothetical $100 million portfolio split equally between them, adding the reported figures suggests almost no net sensitivity (+$0.09 million); harmonising the reporting conventions implies an estimated value change of about-$5.7 million for a parallel 100 basis point rise in rates. The cause is Form N-PORT itself, which asks for DV100, "the change in value of the portfolio resulting from a 100 basis point change in interest rates", without saying whether rates rise or fall. Using every public N-PORT filing from 2019Q4 to 2026Q3, we show that 48% of 53,603 plain long-only bond fund-quarters report a positive DV100 and 52% a negative one across the full sample, with the positive share ranging from 43% to 50% by quarter. The choice is made by the fund complex: 99.0% of registrant-quarters with at least three plain funds are unanimous, and a fund's sign is predicted by its siblings with 99.8% accuracy at 80.2% coverage. A separate re-implementation reproduces the census. Read as filed, 49.2% of cross-complex fund pairs show apparently offsetting rate exposures, against 4.0% once signs are harmonised. In a secondary analysis, harmonising signs and units together lowers the conditional prediction error of monthly fund returns; a pre-registered test of the per-currency detail that a pending SEC proposal would remove is inconclusive. We provide code that builds fund-complex convention lookup tables, and propose a one-sentence clarification to the form.

detail.abstract: Employment law in several systems protects workers against psychological harm caused by work, yet the psychological costs generated by administrative dysfunction (rule-generated workload, contradictory procedural demands, and the displacement of purposes by routines) are seldom the object of legal attention as such. This article asks through which legal gateways those costs become cognizable on the employer's side, and what the structure of those gateways reveals about which costs the law is able to see. The study is doctrinal, comparative and interdisciplinary. It reviews organizational-psychology and public-administration evidence on red tape, administrative burden, job strain and burnout; it examines three systems chosen for the different gateways they emphasize: England and Wales (negligence liability for stress-related psychiatric injury), France (the 2025 recognition of institutional moral harassment by the Cour de cassation) and Brazil (the inclusion of psychosocial risk factors in occupational risk management under NR-1, in force from May 2026); and it uses the novel O Prédio que Aprendeu a Escutar as an interpretive case rather than as evidence. The central proposition is that these costs enter employer-side law only after conversion into an individual injury tied to a foreseeable warning sign, a deliberate policy attributable to identifiable decision-makers, or an entry in an organizational risk inventory, and that only the last is structured to address dysfunction itself. Because the documented effects are small to medium and heterogeneous, the analysis favors procedural safeguards, chiefly inventories able to capture procedural sources of strain, over any expansion of substantive liability. Limitations and conditions that would falsify the thesis are stated. detail.abstract: This paper examines evidence for myopia, or cognitive discounting, in macroeconomic models, exploiting information from the term structure of survey expectations. I estimate a Behavioral New Keynesian model, which incorporates, as observable variables, survey forecast data on output, inflation, and interest rates at horizons ranging from one quarter to ten years ahead. When expectations data are excluded, the estimation suggests implausibly large levels of myopia. But when the model is required to match the behavior of expectations in the data, the evidence for myopia largely disappears: the myopia parameter is estimated near one. The extra discounting implied by myopia is, in fact, at odds with the term structure of expectations, which remain quite persistent across horizons, rather than reverting rapidly to steady state. These findings indicate that myopic discounting in New Keynesian frameworks is difficult to reconcile with the dynamics of expectations observed in survey data.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the decline and adaptation of Japan's geisha profession through economic, demographic, and social perspectives. Drawing on historical scholarship, government statistics, and contemporary accounts of geisha communities, it argues that this decline cannot be attributed solely to diminishing interest in traditional culture. The collapse of Japan's asset-price bubble and the prolonged economic stagnation that followed reduced corporate entertainment spending and weakened the patronage networks that had sustained private ozashiki. Simultaneously, low fertility, population aging, and a shrinking youth population narrowed the pool of potential apprentices. Expanding educational and professional opportunities for women further reduced the appeal of a demanding apprenticeship system characterized by strict hierarchies, intensive training, and limited personal autonomy. Despite these pressures, the profession has not disappeared. Surviving geisha communities, particularly those in Kyoto, have adapted through tourism, public performances, digital recruitment, cultural branding, and heritage-preservation initiatives. These strategies have broadened access to geisha arts while creating tensions between authenticity and commercialization, exclusivity and visibility, and tradition and labour reform. This paper concludes that the geisha profession is undergoing not only quantitative decline but also qualitative transformation: from an elite, patronage-based entertainment industry into a cultural-heritage institution increasingly supported by tourists, public audiences, and preservation networks. Its long-term survival will depend on preserving its artistic foundations while reforming institutional practices that conflict with contemporary economic realities and expectations of women's autonomy.

detail.abstract: Trust in the medical system has eroded substantially in recent years, yet its role as a determinant of health and health care use remains understudied. In this paper, I estimate the effect of medical mistrust on health behaviors and sources of health information using NielsenIQ Consumer Panel data. First, I use a causal forest strategy to predict heterogeneous changes in medical mistrust, drawing on plausibly exogenous variation arising from the COVID-19 pandemic. Then, I show that individuals with larger predicted increases in mistrust reduced their use of physicians for both medical treatment and health information and increased their reliance on natural or alternative treatments and online health information. These findings represent the first causal evidence that medical mistrust shapes patient decision-making across a broad, demographically diverse sample, with effects that persist even after accounting for education, income, and race. This shift away from clinical decision makers and toward online information and non-traditional treatments increases patients' exposure to misinformation and to care that lacks professional oversight. Because mistrust operates independently of conventional socioeconomic factors, policies aimed at improving health care access such as reducing costs or expanding insurance coverage, may fail to address the trust problem driving these shifts.

detail.abstract:
This article brings Marxist dependency theory together with the feminist political economy of social reproduction in order to argue that the impossibility of reproducing life in decent conditions is constitutive of dependent capitalism rather than incidental to it. Peripheral position destroys reproductive conditions through five channels: wage compression, fiscal erosion, degradation of the commons, the blocking of sovereign infrastructure, and the subordination of the state. When those conditions collapse, reproduction is displaced onto feminised unpaid labour and global care chains. 

Three theoretical contributions follow. The article identifies a foundational indeterminacy in Marini's framework-the value of labour power cannot be determined without the unpaid reproductive labour that offsets wage compression-and recasts super-exploitation as a tripartite structure. It introduces peripheral structural sub-reproduction as a constitutive condition of dependent insertion, and it defends sovereign reproductive infrastructure as reproductive policy. 

The article proposes the Social Reproduction Index and tests it across a panel of 66 countries from 2000 to 2022. Under country and year fixed effects, reducing dependency improves the structural conditions of reproduction, and the effect is concentrated in the dimension that combines income and infrastructure. The article explores displacement onto feminised unpaid labour in countries with time-use surveys, where the relationship runs in the predicted direction; extending that coverage across the Global South is one of the article's conclusions.

detail.abstract: Reserve-currency transitions are often described as the end point of a widening gap between an issuer's share of world output and its share of world military spending. I formalise that gap as the Hegemony Gap Index (HGI), define the transition lag τ as the time from the index's first sustained negative crossing to formal loss of primacy, and ask whether an issuer's monetary sovereignty µ, scored on a four-item rubric, explains τ across nine historical cases. The paper is an exercise in what so small a sample can and cannot identify. Using closed-form and exhaustively enumerated computations rather than optimiser output, I show that (i) the fitted µ-τ curve is observationally equivalent to a two-group step function (R 2 = 0.704) that predicts better out of sample than a three-parameter curve; (ii) a bootstrap interval for the conditional mean, 41.2-62.2 years, covers a new issuer only 52% of the time, whereas a predictive interval is 15.5-88.5 years; (iii) µ = 1 coincides exactly with reserve-issuer status (Fisher exact p = 0.0079), and a simple pre-1900/post-1900 split fits the lags better than µ does, so sovereignty cannot be separated from reserve status or era; and (iv) results are fragile to the dating of transitions and to scoring errors. The four reserve issuers in the sample took decades, not years, to lose primacy (exact permutation p = 0.0238); the sample supports no more than that, and no date for any future transition. I also specify, but do not report, a blind re-scoring protocol for the rubric, a rule-based comparison sample that includes censored cases, and an out-of-sample market test.
